Science.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
Science.summary: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies.

Science.title: Why disaster risks are systemic and co-evolutionary
Science.summary: Disasters rarely happen in isolation. New research highlights the need to rethink how we assess disaster risks by recognizing how natural hazards, the people and places exposed, and their vulnerability are interconnected and change over time.

Science.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

Science.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
Science.summary: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science. The findings, published in Planetary and Space Science, come as the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission entered orbit around Mercury this week.

Science.title: Named 'Maria,' a new species of amphibian pays tribute to the world's most popular name
Science.summary: Maria, the most popular female name in Brazil and around the world, was chosen for a new species of caecilian, a type of amphibian commonly known as a "blind snake," found in this South American country. The researchers chose the name Siphonops maria to raise awareness of this little-known animal, even among researchers in the field.

Science.title: Mini microscope captures brain activity while mice are on the go
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03380-w A head-mounted device records neuronal activity as mice explore a naturalistic environment and interact with each other. Specialists discuss the technology and its applications.

Science.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
Science.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

Science.title: How acidic compounds in human sweat open a mosquito ion channel
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03381-9 Structures of a mosquito receptor bound to acids from human skin could inspire tactics to stifle the attraction of malaria-carrying mosquitoes to humans.

Science.title: Flexible simulations model how dark matter collisions may leave their fingerprints on the universe
Science.summary: We cannot see or measure dark matter directly. Yet scientists are convinced that it exists and that it accounts for around 85% of all matter in the universe, including the matter that everything here on Earth is made of, from earthworms and mountains to seawater and washing machines.

Science.title: A common language for pistachio growth: Researchers develop a crop-monitoring scale
Science.summary: The pistachio BBCH scale, created by the University of Córdoba, standardizes phenological monitoring of the crop, enabling researchers and farmers to identify its growth stage quickly and easily.

Science.title: Body-positive imagery in ads resonates differently with men and women, study finds
Science.summary: Advocates of body-positive advertising, which showcases models who do not fit the traditional molds of thin or muscular models, say they are challenging female beauty standards by rejecting an unhealthy obsession with often unattainable idealized bodies. However, a new Concordia study shows that while women generally respond positively to large-size models, body-positive advertising images are not as effective with men.

Science.title: Who did figure 3? Why scientists should make experimental contributions visible
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03542-w Research papers rarely make plain which authors performed which experiments. That’s a missed opportunity, says Tito Calì.

Science.title: Evolution keeps returning to simple leaves
Science.summary: A study led by researchers from the University of Oxford has explained a long-standing riddle: why do most plants have leaves with a very simple shape? In a new study published Nov. 24, they explain why complex leaves have evolved again and again—only for evolution to repeatedly revert to simpler forms.

Science.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
Science.summary: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Science.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
Science.summary: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status.

Science.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
Science.summary: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no higher. As such trees decline across Europe, it is important to understand what they contribute to the soil. The results were published in the journal Agroforestry Systems.
